title: The network that melts at 09:00
tagline: Every morning the office VLAN saturates for twenty minutes. No one changed anything. Two switches, two links, no loop protection.
environment: Two access switches, SW1 and SW2
Two uplinks between them, both in VLAN 10
No STP configured on either switch
topology:
SW1 ==(Gi0/1)====(Gi0/1)== SW2
SW1 ==(Gi0/2)====(Gi0/2)== SW2
workstations on both switches, all in VLAN 10
symptoms: Connectivity collapses for 10-20 minutes each morning, then recovers on its own
Switch CPU sits at 100% and the management interface is barely reachable
All link LEDs blink in unison at high rate
The outage correlates with people arriving and powering on laptops
objectives: Recognise a broadcast storm from its signature rather than from a user description
Explain how a Layer 2 loop amplifies a single broadcast into saturation
Choose the correct structural fix and understand why a workaround is not one
framework: Is the problem bandwidth, or is the same frame being repeated?
Is the MAC table stable, or are entries moving between ports?
Is there more than one active path between the same two Layer 2 devices?

evidence.label: Interface counters during the incident
evidence.output:
5 minute input rate 941200000 bits/sec, 183000 packets/sec
  5 minute output rate 941100000 bits/sec, 183000 packets/sec
     broadcasts 41822311
evidence.insight: 941 Mbps on a 1 Gbps link with 183k packets/sec and 41 million broadcasts. This is not user traffic; it is a flood of broadcast frames.

evidence.label: MAC table behaviour
evidence.insight: The same MAC appears on two ports, and it will keep moving. MAC flapping between the two uplinks is the definitive signature of a loop.

evidence.label: Is loop protection running?
evidence.insight: With STP disabled, both uplinks forward simultaneously, so the two switches form a cycle. Every broadcast is duplicated forever.

evidence.label: What the frames actually are
evidence.output:
10:02:11.001 ARP, Request who-has 10.0.10.1 tell 10.0.10.11, length 28
10:02:11.001 ARP, Request who-has 10.0.10.1 tell 10.0.10.11, length 28
10:02:11.002 ARP, Request who-has 10.0.10.1 tell 10.0.10.11, length 28
10:02:11.002 ARP, Request who-has 10.0.10.1 tell 10.0.10.11, length 28
evidence.insight: The same ARP request repeated within the same millisecond, with identical content. A single broadcast is being multiplied by the loop, not generated by a broken host.

evidence.label: Switch CPU and control-plane health
evidence.output:
CPU utilization for five seconds: 99%/0%; one minute: 98%; five minutes: 61%
  PID Runtime(ms)   Invoked  uSecs   5Sec   1Min   5Min TTY Process
   42    88213322  18822311   4687  71.0%  70.2%  44.1%  0 Spanning Tree
  118    9922110   2211334   4487  18.0%  17.9%  11.2%  0 ARP Input
evidence.insight: The control plane is saturated by broadcast processing. This is why the management interface is barely reachable — the switch is busy, not broken.

evidence.label: Why it recovers by itself
evidence.output:
*Nov 17 09:21:04: %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface Gi0/2, changed state to down
*Nov 17 09:21:04: %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface Gi0/2, changed state to up
evidence.insight: The second uplink flapped, breaking the cycle. Recovery is accidental, not a fix — the loop returns the next time both links are up.

hypotheses.text: A workstation is infected and flooding the network.
hypotheses.why: The repeated frames are identical copies of one broadcast, and the MAC table shows the same address on two ports — a topology loop, not a chatty host.

hypotheses.text: There is a Layer 2 loop between the two switches because both uplinks forward and STP is disabled.
hypotheses.why: Two parallel links, STP disabled, MAC flapping, 41M broadcasts and 99% control-plane CPU all point to the same cause.

hypotheses.text: The uplink is oversubscribed by legitimate traffic.
hypotheses.why: The traffic is broadcast at 183k packets/sec with identical content; user data does not look like that.
The switch recovers the moment one link flaps, which is a topology effect, not a hardware symptom.

solution.root_cause: Two parallel links between SW1 and SW2 both forward in VLAN 10 with spanning tree disabled. The result is a Layer 2 forwarding loop: every broadcast is duplicated and re-circulated, saturating both uplinks and the switches' control planes. The morning correlation is simply when the second link comes up or when the first broadcast of the day is generated.
solution.resolution: Enable RSTP (or MSTP) on both switches and both uplinks so one link is placed in a blocking state, and enable BPDU Guard on all access ports so a user device cannot inject spanning tree. If the two links are meant to carry traffic together, configure a LAG/LACP bundle instead — that gives redundancy and aggregate bandwidth without a loop.
solution.verification: show spanning-tree shows one uplink forwarding and one blocking (or a single Po1 bundle); the MAC table shows each address on exactly one port; broadcast counters stop climbing; switch CPU returns to single digits; and a capture shows each broadcast once.
lessons: A loop is a topology defect, not a traffic defect. Fix the topology.
MAC flapping between two ports is the fastest single indicator of a Layer 2 loop.
Self-recovery is a warning sign, not reassurance: the loop will return when the topology does.
interview_followups: What is the difference between STP blocking a port and a port being down?
Why is a LAG better than two separate links between the same switches?
What does BPDU Guard protect against?

resolution_options.text: Enable RSTP on both switches and both uplinks
resolution_options.why: Breaks the cycle by blocking one path while keeping it available as a standby.

resolution_options.text: Bundle the two uplinks into a LAG with LACP
resolution_options.why: Also correct: a bundle is a single logical link, so there is no loop and both links carry traffic.

resolution_options.text: Enable BPDU Guard on access ports
resolution_options.why: Prevents a user device or a misconfigured switch from creating a loop at the edge.

resolution_options.text: Shut down the second uplink permanently
resolution_options.why: Removes redundancy and leaves the design undocumented; the next person re-enables it and the storm returns.

resolution_options.text: Rate-limit broadcast traffic on the uplinks
resolution_options.why: Masks the symptom while the loop keeps consuming capacity and the MAC table keeps flapping.

interview_questions.q: How do you recognise a broadcast storm in under a minute?
interview_questions.a: Interface counters show near-line-rate broadcast traffic, the MAC table shows the same address on multiple ports, and switch CPU is saturated by broadcast/STP processing. Any one of those is suggestive; all three is conclusive.

It elects a root bridge, computes a loop-free tree, and blocks redundant ports. Blocked ports still receive BPDUs so they can take over if the active path fails. RSTP converges in seconds rather than the 30-50 seconds of classic STP.

interview_questions.q: Why can a loop take down a whole VLAN rather than just one link?
interview_questions.a: Broadcasts are flooded to every port in the VLAN, so each copy is multiplied across the loop and re-flooded. The amplification consumes all capacity in the broadcast domain and saturates the switches' CPUs, which also affects management and other VLANs on the same device.
